question: Laws of motion mainly connect the motion of a body with what physical cause?
opt_a: The colour and shape of the body
opt_b: The temperature of the surroundings only
opt_d: The path length already covered by the body
explanation: Laws of motion explain why the state of motion of a body changes. The immediate physical cause studied in laws of motion is force, which arises from interaction between bodies. A body may be pushed, pulled, attracted by Earth, or slowed by contact with another surface. These are different examples of forces, but each can change speed, direction, or both. Colour and shape may describe the body, but they do not by themselves explain its acceleration. The main shift here is from describing motion to finding the interaction responsible for changing it.

question: A car is described as moving with speed \(20\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) along a straight road. This statement belongs most directly to
explanation: Kinematics describes motion using quantities such as position, displacement, velocity, speed, and acceleration. The statement only says how fast the car is moving and gives no information about the force producing or changing that motion. Dynamics goes one step further and asks why the motion changes, usually through forces and Newton’s laws. A straight-road speed value does not automatically mean friction is being analysed. The same value \(20\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) can be used in dynamics later, but by itself it is only a description of motion.

question: A person pulls a cart using a rope. In this situation, the pull on the cart is best described as
opt_a: a property stored permanently inside the cart
opt_b: the distance travelled by the cart per second
opt_c: an interaction between the rope and the cart
opt_d: the mass of the cart converted into motion
explanation: A force is not an isolated property of a single body in the way mass is. It appears when two bodies interact, such as a rope pulling a cart or Earth attracting a stone. The cart experiences a pull because the rope interacts with it along the direction of the rope. Speed or distance per second describes motion, not the cause of motion. The mass of the cart affects how much acceleration the force can produce, but mass itself is not the pulling interaction.

question: The symbol \(\vec{F}\) is used instead of only \(F\) when the force is being treated as
explanation: The arrow over \(\vec{F}\) shows that force is being treated as a vector quantity. A vector has both magnitude and direction, so two forces of the same size can produce different effects if they act in different directions. Writing only \(F\) often refers to magnitude when direction is either known or not being emphasized. The unit of force is \( \text{N} \), not \( \text{kg} \). Direction matters in laws of motion because the acceleration produced by a net force is along the direction of that net force.

question: The SI unit relation for force is completed by \(1\,\text{N}=1\,\_\_\_\_\).
explanation: The SI unit of force is newton, written as \( \text{N} \). From the relation \(F=ma\), mass has unit \( \text{kg} \) and acceleration has unit \( \text{m s}^{-2} \). Therefore the unit of force becomes \( \text{kg m s}^{-2} \). The option \( \text{kg m s}^{-1} \) is related to momentum, not force. The power \( \text{s}^{-2} \) is important because force is connected with acceleration, not just velocity.

question: Use the arrangement described below: a box is pushed \(8\,\text{N}\) east and at the same time pulled \(3\,\text{N}\) west along the same straight line. What is the net force on the box?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given forces:} \) \(8\,\text{N}\) east and \(3\,\text{N}\) west.
\( \textbf{Direction choice:} \) Take east as positive and west as negative.
\( \textbf{Net force relation:} \)
\[\sum F = F_{\text{east}}-F_{\text{west}}\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[\sum F = 8\,\text{N}-3\,\text{N}\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[\sum F = 5\,\text{N}\]
The positive sign means the resultant force is toward the east.
Adding \(8\,\text{N}\) and \(3\,\text{N}\) would ignore their opposite directions.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The net force is \(5\,\text{N}\) east.

question: A body at rest starts moving when pushed. The most suitable description of this change is that the force has changed the body’s
explanation: A body at rest has zero velocity relative to the chosen reference frame. When a push makes it start moving, its velocity changes from zero to a non-zero value. This change in velocity means a change in state of motion. A force can produce such a change when the forces on the body are not balanced. The push does not normally change the amount of matter in the body. Laws of motion focus on the relation between force and change of motion, not on chemical change.

question: In a bicycle moving along a road, applying brakes mainly causes a change in motion because
explanation: Brakes create a retarding interaction that opposes the motion of the bicycle. This force reduces the bicycle’s velocity, so the bicycle has acceleration opposite to its direction of motion. A change in speed is a change in motion and therefore belongs naturally to dynamics. The mass of the bicycle is not removed during braking. Acceleration can be negative relative to a chosen positive direction, so slowing down is still accelerated motion.

question:
Match the symbols with their usual meanings in laws of motion.
SymbolMeaning
P. \(\vec{F}\)1. Linear momentum
Q. \(m\)2. Acceleration
R. \(\vec{a}\)3. Force
S. \(\vec{p}\)4. Mass
The best matching is
explanation: The symbol \(\vec{F}\) represents force, and the arrow indicates that force is a vector quantity. The symbol \(m\) represents mass, which is a scalar quantity measured in \( \text{kg} \). The symbol \(\vec{a}\) represents acceleration, the rate of change of velocity. The symbol \(\vec{p}\) represents linear momentum, which connects motion with mass through \(\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\). Distinguishing \(\vec{a}\) from \(\vec{p}\) matters because acceleration describes change of velocity, while momentum combines mass with velocity.

question: A stone falling vertically near Earth changes its speed mainly because
opt_a: its mass becomes zero while falling
opt_b: time acts upward on the stone
opt_c: velocity is always directed downward for every body
opt_d: Earth exerts a gravitational force on it
explanation: A falling stone is acted upon by Earth’s gravitational force. This force is directed vertically downward and changes the stone’s velocity. The stone’s mass does not become zero during the fall; mass is a property of the body. Time is not a force and cannot act upward or downward. The direction of velocity depends on the motion, but the cause of the changing velocity in this case is the gravitational interaction with Earth.

question:
Study the table and identify the row that best separates kinematics from dynamics.
RowKinematicsDynamics
PDescribes motionExplains motion using forces
QExplains forcesIgnores acceleration
RDeals only with restDeals only with circular motion
SUses only massUses only time
explanation: Kinematics describes motion using quantities such as displacement, velocity, and acceleration. It does not ask what interaction produced that motion. Dynamics studies the causes of motion and relates force to the change in motion. Row P captures this difference without excluding any valid kind of motion. Dynamics does not ignore acceleration; acceleration is central to Newton’s second law. A clean separation is that kinematics describes the motion, while dynamics explains the motion through forces.

question: A force of \(1\,\text{N}\) acting on a mass of \(1\,\text{kg}\) produces what acceleration when no other force acts?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Force \(F=1\,\text{N}\) and mass \(m=1\,\text{kg}\).
\( \textbf{Required:} \) Acceleration \(a\).
\( \textbf{Unit relation:} \)
\[1\,\text{N}=1\,\text{kg m s}^{-2}\]
\( \textbf{Newton’s second-law form:} \)
\[F=ma\]
\( \textbf{Rearranging:} \)
\[a=\frac{F}{m}\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[a=\frac{1\,\text{N}}{1\,\text{kg}}\]
\( \textbf{Using the newton definition:} \)
\[a=\frac{1\,\text{kg m s}^{-2}}{1\,\text{kg}}=1\,\text{m s}^{-2}\]
The unit \( \text{m s}^{-1} \) would describe velocity, not acceleration.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The acceleration is \(1\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).

question: A force is completely specified only when its magnitude is given along with
explanation: Force is a vector quantity, so magnitude alone is not enough to describe it completely. A force of \(10\,\text{N}\) east and a force of \(10\,\text{N}\) west have the same magnitude but different effects on the body. The direction decides how the force combines with other forces and what acceleration it tends to produce. Colour and temperature may be physical properties in other contexts, but they do not complete the description of a force vector. This is why symbols such as \(\vec{F}\) are useful when direction is important.

question: A block is pulled to the right by \(6\,\text{N}\) and pushed to the right by another \(4\,\text{N}\). With no other horizontal force, the resultant horizontal force is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given horizontal forces:} \) \(6\,\text{N}\) right and \(4\,\text{N}\) right.
\( \textbf{Direction check:} \) Both forces act along the same line and in the same direction.
\( \textbf{Resultant relation:} \)
\[\sum F = 6\,\text{N}+4\,\text{N}\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[\sum F = 10\,\text{N}\]
The direction remains to the right because both contributing forces point right.
Subtracting the forces would be suitable only if they acted in opposite directions.
Multiplying \(6\) and \(4\) has no meaning for finding the resultant of two collinear forces.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The resultant horizontal force is \(10\,\text{N}\) right.

question:
Two descriptions are given below.
I. A ball changes its direction while moving around a curve.
II. A cart speeds up when pulled forward.
What do both descriptions have in common?
opt_a: Both require the mass of the object to become zero
opt_b: Both describe motion without any possible force
opt_c: Both involve a change in the state of motion
opt_d: Both prove that direction is not important in mechanics
explanation: A change in the state of motion can mean a change in speed, a change in direction, or both. In statement I, the direction of velocity changes as the ball moves around a curve. In statement II, the speed changes as the cart speeds up. Both changes require attention to dynamics when the cause is being studied. The mass of the object need not become zero in either case. Direction is especially important in mechanics because velocity, acceleration, and force are vector quantities.

question: A reference frame is needed in describing motion because
opt_a: force loses its direction in any frame
opt_b: motion is relative to a frame
opt_c: mass changes its SI unit between frames
opt_d: time cannot be measured in mechanics
explanation: Motion is described relative to a chosen reference frame. A passenger sitting inside a moving bus is at rest relative to the bus but moving relative to the ground. The description of velocity and acceleration must therefore mention or imply a frame of reference. Force remains a vector quantity and does not lose its direction because a frame is chosen. The SI unit of mass remains \( \text{kg} \), so the role of the frame is about describing motion, not changing basic units.

question: In the early study of laws of motion, mass is introduced as a quantity connected with
explanation: Mass is closely related to inertia, which is the resistance of a body to change in its state of motion. A body with greater mass is harder to start, stop, or deflect by the same applied force. This does not mean mass is a force; rather, it measures how strongly a body resists acceleration. Brightness and clock time do not measure this resistance. This link between mass and inertia prepares the meaning of Newton’s laws without confusing mass with weight.

question: A heavy trolley and a light trolley are initially at rest on a smooth horizontal floor. The same horizontal force acts on each for the same short time. The lighter trolley is expected to
opt_a: remain exactly at rest because it is lighter
opt_b: have greater inertia than the heavy trolley
opt_c: show a larger change in motion
opt_d: experience no force because the floor is smooth
explanation: For the same applied force, a smaller mass offers less resistance to change in motion. The lighter trolley therefore gains acceleration more easily than the heavier trolley. Smoothness of the floor only suggests that friction may be small; it does not remove the applied force. The heavier trolley has greater inertia because inertia increases with mass. The comparison is not about which trolley has a force acting on it, but about how much its motion changes under the same force.

question:
Forces are listed below.
CaseDescriptionType of interaction
PA hand pushes a doorContact interaction
QEarth pulls a falling stoneNon-contact interaction
RA string pulls a small blockContact interaction through the string
SA magnet attracts an iron pinNon-contact interaction
Which case pairs are classified suitably?
explanation: A push by a hand on a door is a contact force because the bodies touch. A string pulling a block is also treated as a contact interaction transmitted through the string. Earth’s gravitational pull on a stone does not require contact, so it is a non-contact interaction. A magnet can attract an iron pin without touching it, so it is also a non-contact interaction. The important separation is not whether the force is visible, but whether physical contact is needed for that interaction.

question: A notebook says that weight is “the force with which Earth attracts a body.” The best unit for this quantity is
explanation: Weight is a force, so its SI unit is the newton, \( \text{N} \). Mass is measured in \( \text{kg} \), but weight is not the same quantity as mass. Near Earth, the magnitude of weight is commonly written as \(W=mg\), where \(m\) is mass and \(g\) is acceleration due to gravity. Since \(m\) has unit \( \text{kg} \) and \(g\) has unit \( \text{m s}^{-2} \), the product has unit \( \text{kg m s}^{-2}=\text{N} \). The unit \( \text{m s}^{-1} \) belongs to velocity, while \( \text{s} \) belongs to time.

question: A block is acted upon by forces \(12\,\text{N}\) east, \(5\,\text{N}\) west, and \(4\,\text{N}\) east along the same horizontal line. The net force on the block is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Forces along one line:} \) Eastward forces are \(12\,\text{N}\) and \(4\,\text{N}\), while the westward force is \(5\,\text{N}\).
\( \textbf{Sign choice:} \) Take east as positive and west as negative.
\( \textbf{Net-force expression:} \)
\[\sum F = 12\,\text{N}+4\,\text{N}-5\,\text{N}\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[\sum F = 16\,\text{N}-5\,\text{N}=11\,\text{N}\]
The positive value means the resultant force is eastward.
Adding all magnitudes would ignore direction, while subtracting \(12\,\text{N}\) from \(5\,\text{N}\) would miss the second eastward force.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The net force is \(11\,\text{N}\) east.

question: A book rests on a horizontal table. Earth pulls the book downward, and the table pushes the book upward. These two forces are mentioned here mainly to show that
opt_a: every force must be a non-contact force
opt_b: upward forces are always larger than downward forces
opt_c: different interactions can act on the same body
opt_d: contact forces do not have direction
explanation: The book is acted on by more than one force at the same time. Earth exerts the gravitational force, or weight, downward on the book. The table exerts a contact force, called normal reaction, upward on the book. Both forces act on the same body, so they must be considered together when discussing the book’s motion. Contact forces and non-contact forces can both be vector quantities. The upward force is not always larger; for a book at rest on a horizontal table, the upward and downward forces have equal magnitudes.

question: The dimension of force can be obtained from \(F=ma\). It is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Relation used:} \)
\[F=ma\]
\( \textbf{Dimension of mass:} \)
\[[m]=[M]\]
\( \textbf{Dimension of acceleration:} \)
\[[a]=[LT^{-2}]\]
\( \textbf{Combining dimensions:} \)
\[[F]=[m][a]\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[[F]=[M][LT^{-2}]\]
\( \textbf{Result:} \)
\[[F]=[MLT^{-2}]\]
The dimension \([MLT^{-1}]\) belongs to momentum, not force.
The extra power \(T^{-2}\) appears because force is linked with acceleration.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The dimension of force is \([MLT^{-2}]\).

question: A force is called a net force when it represents
opt_a: only the largest force acting on the body
opt_b: only the force that acts for the longest time
opt_c: the mass of the body multiplied by its speed
opt_d: the vector sum of all forces acting on the body
explanation: Several forces can act on a body at the same time. The net force, or resultant force, is found by adding those forces as vectors. This means both magnitude and direction must be considered. The largest force alone may not decide the motion if other forces partly oppose or support it. Force multiplied by time later connects with impulse, while mass multiplied by speed is related to momentum magnitude only when direction is not being discussed. In Newton’s laws, the acceleration is linked to the net external force, not to one randomly selected force.

question: A hockey puck slides on a nearly frictionless horizontal surface after being hit once. After it leaves the stick, it continues moving mainly because
opt_a: a forward force must remain stored inside it
opt_b: its weight stops acting during horizontal motion
opt_d: no large opposing force quickly stops it
explanation: The older idea that a force is needed to maintain motion is not consistent with Newtonian mechanics. Once the puck is set in motion, it can continue with nearly constant velocity if the net horizontal force is nearly zero. On a nearly frictionless surface, there is very little opposing force to reduce its motion. The weight of the puck still acts downward, but it is balanced by the normal reaction of the surface in the vertical direction. Motion does not require a stored forward force inside the puck. The key point is that force is needed to change motion, not to merely keep uniform straight-line motion.

question: A cart moving on a rough floor gradually comes to rest after being pushed and released. The best explanation is that
opt_a: friction provides an opposing force after the push is removed
opt_b: the cart stops because moving bodies naturally lose their force
opt_c: the cart’s mass disappears slowly during motion
opt_d: velocity becomes impossible without a continuous push
explanation: When the cart is released, the hand no longer provides a forward push. The rough floor exerts friction on the cart, and this friction acts opposite to the cart’s relative motion. Because of this unbalanced opposing force, the cart slows down and eventually stops. The stopping is not proof that force is always needed to maintain motion. It shows that ordinary surfaces often provide friction, which changes the motion. If friction were negligible, the cart would continue moving much longer with nearly constant velocity.

question:
Read the situation below and answer the question.
A small toy car is pushed briefly on two horizontal tracks. Track P is rough, and the car stops quickly. Track Q is very smooth, and the car moves much farther before slowing noticeably.
What conclusion is best supported by this comparison?
opt_a: Smooth tracks make the car independent of inertia
opt_b: smaller opposing force lets the car move farther
opt_c: A body can move only while a hand is touching it
explanation: The comparison separates the effect of friction from the idea of motion itself. On the rough track, friction is larger, so the car loses speed quickly. On the very smooth track, friction is smaller, so the same kind of car continues moving for a longer distance. This supports the idea that ordinary objects stop because of opposing forces such as friction. It does not show that continuous contact by a hand is required for motion. The car’s mass is not being converted into force; the difference lies in the horizontal resistive interaction with the surface.

question:
Assertion: A body can move with constant velocity even when the net force on it is zero.
Reason: Zero net force means zero acceleration, not necessarily zero velocity.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: A zero net force does not mean the body must be at rest. It means the body has no acceleration, so its velocity does not change. If the body is already at rest, it remains at rest; if it is already moving uniformly in a straight line, it continues with that same velocity. The Reason directly explains why the Assertion is true. Confusing zero force with zero velocity is a common misunderstanding of the first-law idea. The correct link is between net force and change of velocity, not between net force and the mere existence of velocity.

question:
The table below compares two ideas about motion.
RowClaim about motionNewtonian view
PForce is always required to maintain uniform straight-line motionRejected
QForce is required to change velocityAccepted
RFriction can make ordinary moving bodies stopAccepted
SZero net force always means zero speedAccepted
The row that contains a wrong Newtonian view is
explanation: Row P is suitable because Newtonian mechanics rejects the idea that a force is always needed to maintain uniform straight-line motion. Row Q is also suitable because a force is needed to change velocity, meaning to produce acceleration. Row R correctly identifies friction as the reason many ordinary moving bodies slow down and stop. Row S is wrong because zero net force means zero acceleration, not necessarily zero speed. A body moving at constant velocity can have zero net force. The distinction between speed and acceleration is essential when interpreting Newton’s first-law idea.

question: A ball rolls with constant velocity on a long, level, nearly frictionless track. The net horizontal force on the ball is best described as
opt_c: opposite to velocity and very large
explanation: Constant velocity means that the ball’s speed and direction are not changing. If velocity is constant, acceleration is zero. In Newtonian reasoning, zero acceleration corresponds to zero net force along that direction. On a nearly frictionless level track, the opposing horizontal force is very small, so the net horizontal force is zero or nearly zero. The weight acts vertically downward and is not the net horizontal force. A large force opposite to velocity would make the ball slow down noticeably.

question:
Consider the statements below.
I. A force is needed to start a body from rest.
II. A force is needed to stop a moving body.
III. A force is always needed to keep a body moving with constant velocity.
Which set agrees with the Newtonian idea of force?
explanation: Starting a body from rest requires a change in velocity, so a net force is needed. Stopping a moving body also requires a change in velocity, so a net force is again needed. But a body already moving with constant velocity does not require a net force to keep moving in that same way. In real life, friction often acts, so a continuous push may be needed to balance friction and maintain constant speed. That practical case should not be mistaken for the basic law: when the net force is zero, uniform straight-line motion can continue.

question: A smooth puck moves in a straight line with nearly constant speed after a short push. A rough patch is then placed in its path, and the puck slows while crossing it. This change occurs because the rough patch
opt_a: changes the puck’s velocity without applying any force
opt_c: creates a force opposite to the relative motion
opt_d: makes the puck’s weight act horizontally forward
explanation: The puck initially moves nearly uniformly because the horizontal opposing force is small. When it reaches the rough patch, friction becomes appreciable. Friction acts opposite to the relative sliding or tendency of sliding between the puck and surface. This opposing force produces acceleration opposite to the motion, so the puck slows down. The puck’s inertia is not removed; it still resists change in its state of motion. The weight of the puck continues to act vertically downward and does not become a forward horizontal force.

question: In Galileo’s inertia idea, an ideal object moving on a perfectly smooth horizontal surface with no opposing force would
opt_b: gradually stop because motion must fade
opt_c: move faster and faster without limit
explanation: Galileo’s reasoning helped replace the idea that force is required to maintain motion. If opposing forces such as friction are removed, a moving body need not slow down. It would continue moving with constant velocity in a straight line. This is the basic idea of inertia, later expressed clearly in Newton’s first law. The object would not speed up without a net force because speeding up requires acceleration. The result is not about converting mass into velocity, but about the natural persistence of the state of motion when no net force changes it.

question: A claim says, “A moving body must have a force in the direction of its motion.” The clearest counterexample is
opt_a: a block moving uniformly on a smooth horizontal surface
opt_b: a stone resting on level ground with balanced forces
opt_c: a car speeding up because a forward net force acts
opt_d: a ball slowing down on a rough floor due to friction
explanation: A counterexample must show motion without requiring a forward net force. A block moving at constant velocity on a frictionless horizontal surface has no acceleration, so its net horizontal force is zero. It is still moving, which contradicts the claim that a moving body must have a force along its motion. A stone at rest does not address the case of a moving body. A speeding car has a forward net force, and a slowing ball has an opposing force, so those examples do not challenge the claim. Uniform motion on a frictionless surface is the cleanest way to separate velocity from net force.

question:
A graph description is given below.
For a body moving along a straight line, the velocity-time graph is a horizontal straight line above the time axis.
For this motion, the net force along the line is
opt_c: equal to displacement per unit time
explanation: A horizontal line on a velocity-time graph means the velocity is constant. The slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration. Since the graph is horizontal, the slope is zero, so the acceleration is zero. For constant mass motion along a line, zero acceleration corresponds to zero net force along that line. Non-zero velocity alone does not require non-zero net force. The graph shows uniform motion, and the physical reading is that no resultant force is changing the velocity.

question: A box initially moving east experiences no net force after a certain instant. Its later motion, as predicted by the inertia idea, is
opt_a: uniform motion east with the same velocity
opt_c: uniform motion west with the same speed
opt_d: accelerated motion east with increasing speed
explanation: If the net force becomes zero, the acceleration becomes zero. Zero acceleration means the velocity stops changing from that instant onward. Since the box was already moving east, it continues moving east with the same velocity. It does not stop immediately unless an opposing force acts long enough to reduce its velocity to zero. It also does not reverse direction without a force causing that change. Inertia preserves the current state of motion when no net external force alters it.

question: A smooth table has a puck moving north at constant speed. Later, a brief sideways push acts toward east. After the push, the puck’s motion changes mainly because
opt_a: force can change the direction of velocity
opt_b: force acts only opposite to motion
opt_d: a body at constant speed cannot be affected by force
explanation: Velocity is a vector, so changing its direction is also a change in motion. A sideways push gives the puck an acceleration toward the east during the time of contact. This changes the velocity vector even if the speed change is not the main focus. A force need not act only opposite to motion; it may act along, opposite to, or at an angle to the velocity. Constant speed before the push does not make the puck immune to forces. The example shows why laws of motion must treat direction as carefully as magnitude.

question: An object moves in a straight line with constant speed on a surface where friction is negligible. The statement that best repairs the old “force-as-motion” idea is
opt_a: force is needed for velocity, not for acceleration
opt_b: force is another name for speed
opt_c: force disappears whenever mass is large
opt_d: force changes velocity, not velocity itself
explanation: The older view treated force as something needed to keep a body moving. Newtonian mechanics instead connects net force with acceleration, which is change in velocity. A body can have velocity even when its acceleration is zero. If friction is negligible and no other horizontal force acts, the body can keep moving uniformly. Force is not the same quantity as speed, because force is a vector interaction with unit \( \text{N} \), while speed has unit \( \text{m s}^{-1} \). The repaired idea is that net force changes motion rather than simply accompanying motion.

question: A child pushes a toy car, releases it, and sees it stop after a short distance on the floor. Another child says, “It stopped because no forward force remained.” A better explanation is that
opt_a: the absence of forward force alone proves stopping
opt_b: friction reduced the toy car’s velocity
opt_c: the toy car stopped because velocity has no inertia
opt_d: the downward weight pushed it backward
explanation: After release, the forward push from the hand is no longer acting. But the car does not stop merely because a forward force is absent. It stops because friction from the floor acts opposite to its motion and changes its velocity. If the same toy car moved on a much smoother surface, it would continue for a longer time. Weight acts vertically downward and is not the backward horizontal force responsible for slowing. The situation is a practical example of friction hiding the inertia idea in everyday observations.

question: A body moving with velocity \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) along a straight line has zero acceleration for \(4\,\text{s}\). During this interval, the net force along the line is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) The acceleration along the line is \(0\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).
\( \textbf{Relevant idea:} \) Net force is linked with acceleration, not with the mere presence of velocity.
\( \textbf{Newtonian relation for constant mass:} \)
\[\sum F = ma\]
\( \textbf{Substitution of acceleration:} \)
\[\sum F = m(0)\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[\sum F = 0\]
The given velocity \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) shows the body is moving, but it does not by itself require a net force.
The time interval \(4\,\text{s}\) only tells how long the zero-acceleration condition lasts.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The net force along the line is zero.

question: A magnet attracts an iron pin without touching it. This situation shows that a force can arise from
opt_b: the colour of the iron pin
opt_d: the time shown by a clock
explanation: A force is an interaction between bodies, and physical contact is not always necessary. Magnetic attraction can act even when the magnet and iron pin are separated by a small distance. This makes it a non-contact interaction. Contact forces, such as a hand pushing a door, require touching surfaces. Both contact and non-contact forces can change the state of motion of a body. The important idea is that force is identified through interaction, not only through visible contact.

question: A force of \(10\,\text{N}\) north and a force of \(10\,\text{N}\) south do not produce the same effect on a body because force has
explanation: Force is a vector quantity, so its direction is as important as its magnitude. A \(10\,\text{N}\) force toward north and a \(10\,\text{N}\) force toward south have equal magnitudes but opposite directions. Their effects on acceleration are therefore different. If they act together on the same body along the same line, they can cancel. Treating force only as a number would miss this directional effect. Vector addition is needed whenever more than one force acts on a body.

question: Use the arrangement described below: a box is pulled by \(7\,\text{N}\) toward east and \(9\,\text{N}\) toward north at the same time. What can be said about the resultant force?
opt_a: It must be \(16\,\text{N}\) exactly toward east
opt_b: It is a vector directed between east and north
opt_d: It is zero because the forces are perpendicular
explanation: The two forces act at right angles, so they cannot be added by simple arithmetic along one line. The resultant is obtained by vector addition. Since one force is eastward and the other is northward, the resultant points somewhere between east and north. It is not \(16\,\text{N}\) east because the northward force has not disappeared. It is not \(2\,\text{N}\) north because subtraction is suitable only for opposite collinear forces. Perpendicular forces do not cancel unless their vector sum is zero, which is not possible here with non-zero perpendicular components.

question: A \(3\,\text{kg}\) block is pulled by two horizontal forces: \(14\,\text{N}\) to the right and \(5\,\text{N}\) to the left. If no other horizontal force acts, the horizontal acceleration of the block is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Forces along the horizontal line:} \) \(14\,\text{N}\) right and \(5\,\text{N}\) left.
\( \textbf{Sign convention:} \) Take right as positive.
\( \textbf{Net force:} \)
\[\sum F = 14\,\text{N}-5\,\text{N}=9\,\text{N}\]
The positive sign shows that the net force is to the right.
\( \textbf{Newton’s second-law relation:} \)
\[\sum F=ma\]
\( \textbf{Solving for acceleration:} \)
\[a=\frac{\sum F}{m}\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[a=\frac{9\,\text{N}}{3\,\text{kg}}\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[a=3\,\text{m s}^{-2}\]
Using \(14\,\text{N}+5\,\text{N}\) would ignore the opposite directions of the two forces.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The acceleration is \(3\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) to the right.

question:
Study the table and identify the force classification that is not suitable.
RowSituationClassification
PA hand pushes a tableContact force
QEarth attracts a stoneNon-contact force
RA string pulls a blockContact force
SA book presses a tableNon-contact force
explanation: A hand pushing a table is a contact force because the hand and table touch. Earth attracting a stone is gravitational interaction, which does not require contact, so it is non-contact. A string pulls a block through contact along the string, so it is also treated as a contact force. A book pressing a table occurs because the book and table are in contact. Therefore row S is not suitably classified. The surface interaction between the book and table should be treated as a contact force, not a field force.

question: Two forces act on the same body at the same time. One is \(6\,\text{N}\) east and the other is \(8\,\text{N}\) west. The resultant force is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given forces:} \) \(6\,\text{N}\) east and \(8\,\text{N}\) west.
\( \textbf{Sign choice:} \) Take east as positive and west as negative.
\( \textbf{Vector sum along the line:} \)
\[\sum F=+6\,\text{N}-8\,\text{N}\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[\sum F=-2\,\text{N}\]
The negative sign means the resultant force is toward west.
The magnitude of the resultant is \(2\,\text{N}\).
Adding \(6\,\text{N}\) and \(8\,\text{N}\) would be suitable only if both forces acted in the same direction.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The resultant force is \(2\,\text{N}\) west.

question: A force that one part of a system exerts on another part of the same chosen system is called internal relative to that system. If two blocks connected by a string are treated together as one system, the tension in the string is
opt_b: the weight of the two-block system
opt_d: the only force acting on the system
explanation: Whether a force is internal or external depends on the chosen system. If both connected blocks are included in one system, the tension is an interaction between two parts of that same system. It is therefore internal relative to the two-block system. If only one block were chosen as the system, the tension from the string on that block would be external to that one-body system. Weight is a gravitational force due to Earth and is not the same as tension. This system choice becomes important when deciding which forces affect the acceleration of the whole system.

question:
Match the interaction with the most suitable force description.
InteractionForce description
P. Earth and a falling stone1. Magnetic force
Q. Hand and a wall2. Gravitational force
R. Magnet and iron nail3. Contact push
S. Stretched string and block4. Tension
The suitable matching is
explanation: Earth and a falling stone interact through gravitational force, so P matches \(2\). A hand pushing a wall is a contact push, so Q matches \(3\). A magnet attracting an iron nail is a magnetic force, so R matches \(1\). A stretched string pulls a block through tension, so S matches \(4\). These examples show that force names are linked with the type of interaction producing them. The same body can experience different kinds of forces at once, so identifying the interaction is the safest way to name the force.

question: A \(5\,\text{N}\) force acts east and a \(5\,\text{N}\) force acts north on the same object. The magnitude of the resultant is closest to
explanation:
\( \textbf{Forces given:} \) \(5\,\text{N}\) east and \(5\,\text{N}\) north.
The forces are perpendicular, so their resultant is found using the right-triangle relation.
\( \textbf{Resultant magnitude:} \)
\[R=\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2}\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[R=\sqrt{(5\,\text{N})^2+(5\,\text{N})^2}\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[R=\sqrt{25+25}\,\text{N}\]
\[R=\sqrt{50}\,\text{N}\]
\( \textbf{Numerical value:} \)
\[R\approx 7.1\,\text{N}\]
The result is greater than \(5\,\text{N}\) but less than \(10\,\text{N}\) because the forces are perpendicular, not collinear.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The resultant magnitude is approximately \(7.1\,\text{N}\).

question: A diagram is described in words: a block has arrows \(P\), \(Q\), and \(R\) acting on it. Arrow \(P\) is \(10\,\text{N}\) right, arrow \(Q\) is \(4\,\text{N}\) left, and arrow \(R\) is \(6\,\text{N}\) left. The block’s horizontal net force is
explanation: The rightward force is \(10\,\text{N}\). The two leftward forces together have magnitude \(4\,\text{N}+6\,\text{N}=10\,\text{N}\). Since the total rightward force equals the total leftward force, the horizontal forces balance. The vector sum in the horizontal direction is therefore zero. This does not mean no forces act on the block; it means their resultant along the horizontal line is zero. A body can have several forces acting on it and still have zero net force in a particular direction.

question: Inertia is best described as the tendency of a body to resist
opt_d: change in its state of motion
explanation: Inertia is the resistance of a body to a change in its state of rest or motion. A body at rest tends to remain at rest, and a body moving uniformly tends to keep moving uniformly in a straight line. Inertia is also involved when a body resists change in direction. It is not a force acting on the body, but a property connected with mass. Temperature change and contact are different physical ideas. The phrase “state of motion” includes rest, speed, and direction, so it is broader than only moving or only stopping.

question: Passengers in a bus tend to fall backward when the bus suddenly starts moving forward. This observation is mainly an example of inertia of
explanation: Before the bus starts, the passengers’ bodies are initially at rest relative to the ground and the bus. When the bus suddenly moves forward, the feet in contact with the bus floor are pushed forward. The upper part of the body tends to remain in its previous state of rest for a short time. This makes the passenger appear to fall backward relative to the bus. The effect is not due to inertia of direction, because the main change here is from rest to motion. It illustrates resistance to being set into motion.

question: A person jumps from a slowly moving cart and tends to fall forward on the ground. The most suitable reason is that the person’s body tends to
explanation: While the person is on the moving cart, the body has forward velocity along with the cart. On jumping down, the feet may be slowed suddenly by contact with the ground. The upper part of the body tends to keep moving forward because of inertia of motion. This can make the person fall forward. Gravity acts downward, not backward along the horizontal direction. The situation shows that a moving body resists being stopped suddenly.

question: A cyclist moving along a straight road suddenly turns left. The cyclist’s body tends to continue in the original straight-line direction. This is mainly related to
explanation: A moving body tends to continue in its existing direction of motion unless a force changes that direction. During a sudden turn, the bicycle changes direction because of forces from the road through the tyres. The cyclist’s body tends to keep moving along the earlier straight-line direction for a moment. This is described as inertia of direction. It is not inertia of rest because the cyclist was already moving. Turning does not require mass to disappear; it requires a force to change the direction of velocity.

question:
The table below lists common observations and types of inertia.
RowObservationType of inertia
PA carpet is beaten and dust particles separateInertia of rest
QA passenger falls forward when a moving bus stops suddenlyInertia of motion
RA body tends to keep moving in a straight line during a sudden turnInertia of direction
SA heavier body is generally harder to accelerateInertia decreases with mass
The row that contains an unsuitable explanation is
explanation: Row P is suitable because dust particles tend to remain at rest when the carpet is suddenly moved. Row Q is suitable because a passenger’s body tends to continue moving forward when the bus stops suddenly. Row R correctly describes inertia of direction, where a moving body resists change in direction. Row S is unsuitable because inertia does not decrease with mass. Greater mass means greater inertia, so a heavier body is generally harder to accelerate. The mass-inertia connection is central to comparing how bodies respond to the same force.

question:
Assertion: A heavier body has greater inertia than a lighter body.
Reason: Inertia is measured by mass.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: Inertia is the resistance of a body to a change in its state of motion. Mass is the measure of inertia in elementary mechanics. A body with greater mass resists acceleration more strongly under the same applied force. Therefore a heavier body, when compared under the same gravitational conditions, usually has greater mass and greater inertia. The Reason directly supports the Assertion by giving the physical measure of inertia. The idea should not be confused with speed, because a fast light body need not have more inertia than a slow heavy body.

question: Two trolleys are initially at rest on a smooth floor. Trolley P has mass \(2\,\text{kg}\), and trolley Q has mass \(6\,\text{kg}\). The same horizontal force acts on each trolley separately. Compared with trolley Q, trolley P will have
opt_c: the same acceleration because the force is the same
opt_d: zero acceleration because it is lighter
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given masses:} \) \(m_P=2\,\text{kg}\) and \(m_Q=6\,\text{kg}\).
The same force \(F\) acts on each trolley separately.
\( \textbf{Relation for acceleration:} \)
\[a=\frac{F}{m}\]
For trolley P:
\[a_P=\frac{F}{2}\]
For trolley Q:
\[a_Q=\frac{F}{6}\]
\( \textbf{Ratio:} \)
\[\frac{a_P}{a_Q}=\frac{F/2}{F/6}\]
\[\frac{a_P}{a_Q}=3\]
Trolley P has smaller mass, so it has less inertia and accelerates more under the same force.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) Trolley P has three times the acceleration of trolley Q.

question: A fast-moving table-tennis ball and a slowly moving heavy iron ball are compared only for inertia. The deciding quantity is
explanation: Inertia is measured by mass. A body with greater mass has greater resistance to change in its state of motion. Speed affects momentum, but speed alone is not the measure of inertia. A fast light ball may be moving quickly, yet its inertia can be much smaller than that of a slow heavy ball. Direction can matter for velocity and momentum, but it does not decide the amount of inertia. The comparison separates inertia from other motion quantities that also become important later.

question: During a sudden stop of a moving bus, passengers tend to fall forward. The role of inertia in this event is that the upper part of the body tends to
explanation: Before the stop, passengers are moving forward with the bus. When the bus stops suddenly, the feet in contact with the floor may stop quickly. The upper part of the body tends to continue its forward motion because of inertia of motion. This difference in motion between the lower and upper parts makes the passenger lean or fall forward. The body is not becoming free from gravity; gravity still acts downward. The observation is a direct everyday example of resistance to stopping.

question: A body moving in a circle at constant speed is not in a state of unchanged motion because
opt_a: its mass becomes smaller in a circle
opt_b: its direction of velocity keeps changing
opt_c: its speed must be zero at every point
opt_d: no force can act during circular motion
explanation: Motion is not described by speed alone. Velocity is a vector, so it includes both speed and direction. In circular motion at constant speed, the direction of velocity changes continuously. Therefore the state of motion is changing even though the speed remains constant. This connects with inertia of direction because a body would continue in a straight line unless a force changes its direction. The force needed for circular motion is studied later as the inward net force required to keep changing the velocity direction.

question: Mass is treated as a measure of inertia because it tells how strongly a body resists
opt_b: a change in its state of motion
opt_c: a change in its temperature only
opt_d: a change in the clock reading
explanation: Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or motion. Mass gives a quantitative measure of this resistance. A body with larger mass is harder to start, stop, or change in direction by the same applied force. This does not mean mass itself is a force; it is a property of matter. Colour and clock reading do not measure resistance to acceleration. The mass-inertia link explains why the same push affects a light object more than a heavy object.

question: A \(4\,\text{kg}\) body is taken from Earth to the Moon. Ignoring any loss of material, its mass on the Moon is
opt_b: less than \(4\,\text{kg}\), because gravity is weaker there
opt_d: greater than \(4\,\text{kg}\), because it is farther from Earth
explanation: Mass is the amount of matter measured through inertia, and its SI unit is \( \text{kg} \). Taking a body from Earth to the Moon changes the gravitational field acting on it, but it does not change the amount of matter in the body. Therefore its mass remains \(4\,\text{kg}\). Weight changes because weight depends on gravitational acceleration through \(W=mg\). Confusing mass with weight leads to the wrong idea that mass becomes smaller on the Moon. The body would feel lighter there, but its inertia would still correspond to \(4\,\text{kg}\).

question:
Study the table and identify the row that correctly compares mass and weight.
RowMassWeight
PScalar quantity measured in \( \text{kg} \)Force measured in \( \text{N} \)
QForce measured in \( \text{N} \)Scalar quantity measured in \( \text{kg} \)
RChanges from place to place only because of \(g\)Never depends on \(g\)
SAlways directed downwardHas no direction
explanation: Mass is a scalar quantity and is measured in \( \text{kg} \). Weight is a gravitational force and is measured in \( \text{N} \). Weight has direction, usually vertically downward near Earth, because it is a force. Mass does not become a downward vector just because the body is in a gravitational field. Row R reverses the dependence, since weight depends on \(g\) while mass is independent of location in ordinary mechanics. The safest distinction is that mass measures inertia, while weight is the force of gravity on that mass.

question: Two blocks have masses \(2\,\text{kg}\) and \(8\,\text{kg}\). To give both blocks the same acceleration on a smooth horizontal surface, the force on the \(8\,\text{kg}\) block must be
opt_a: one-fourth of the force on the \(2\,\text{kg}\) block
opt_b: one-half of the force on the \(2\,\text{kg}\) block
opt_c: four times the force on the \(2\,\text{kg}\) block
opt_d: equal to the force on the \(2\,\text{kg}\) block
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given masses:} \) \(m_1=2\,\text{kg}\) and \(m_2=8\,\text{kg}\).
Both blocks must have the same acceleration \(a\).
\( \textbf{Newton’s second-law relation:} \)
\[F=ma\]
For the \(2\,\text{kg}\) block:
\[F_1=2a\]
For the \(8\,\text{kg}\) block:
\[F_2=8a\]
\( \textbf{Force ratio:} \)
\[\frac{F_2}{F_1}=\frac{8a}{2a}=4\]
The larger mass needs a larger force for the same acceleration because it has greater inertia.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The \(8\,\text{kg}\) block needs four times the force.

question:
Assertion: Mass is a scalar quantity.
Reason: Mass has magnitude but no direction in space.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_b: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_c: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: Mass is described by a numerical value and a unit such as \( \text{kg} \). It does not point north, south, upward, or downward. A scalar quantity has magnitude only, while a vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. The Reason correctly gives why mass is treated as scalar. Weight, in contrast, is a force and has direction. This contrast prevents the common mixing of mass \(m\) with weight \(W=mg\).

question: A body has mass \(5\,\text{kg}\) and is placed where \(g=9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\). Its weight is closest to
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Mass \(m=5\,\text{kg}\) and gravitational acceleration \(g=9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).
\( \textbf{Required:} \) Weight \(W\).
Weight is the gravitational force on the body.
\( \textbf{Formula:} \)
\[W=mg\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[W=(5\,\text{kg})(9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2})\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[W=49\,\text{kg m s}^{-2}\]
\( \textbf{Unit conversion:} \)
\[1\,\text{kg m s}^{-2}=1\,\text{N}\]
So,
\[W=49\,\text{N}\]
The value \(5\,\text{kg}\) is mass, not weight.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The weight is \(49\,\text{N}\).

question: A suitcase is difficult to set into motion but, once moving, it is also difficult to stop suddenly. This is because its mass is linked with
opt_a: only its colour and surface shine
opt_b: only its downward weight, never horizontal motion
opt_c: the disappearance of force during motion
opt_d: inertia in both starting and stopping changes
explanation: Inertia is resistance to change in the state of motion. Starting a suitcase from rest changes its velocity from zero to a non-zero value, so inertia resists that change. Stopping the suitcase also changes its velocity, so inertia is involved again. Mass measures this resistance, so a suitcase with greater mass is harder to start and harder to stop. Weight may affect contact forces in some situations, but the basic resistance to change in motion is described by inertia. The same property explains both kinds of difficulty.

question: A learner writes, “An object with greater mass always has greater speed because it has greater inertia.” The physics error in this statement is that
opt_b: inertia is measured only by speed
opt_c: mass has no relation with inertia
explanation: Greater mass means greater inertia, but inertia does not mean a body must be moving faster. Inertia describes resistance to change in the state of motion. A heavy object may be at rest, moving slowly, or moving fast depending on the forces and past motion involved. Speed is a kinematic quantity measured in \( \text{m s}^{-1} \), while mass is measured in \( \text{kg} \). The statement wrongly converts resistance to change into a claim about speed. A large mass can have large inertia even when its speed is zero.

question: In the relation \(F=ma\), if the same force acts on bodies of different masses, the body with larger mass gets smaller acceleration because
opt_a: larger mass removes the applied force
opt_b: acceleration does not depend on force
opt_d: force becomes a scalar only for heavy bodies
explanation: The relation \(F=ma\) can be rearranged as \(a=\frac{F}{m}\) for a given net force. If \(F\) is fixed, increasing \(m\) decreases \(a\). This mathematical result matches the physical idea of inertia. A larger mass resists change in motion more strongly, so the same force produces less acceleration. The applied force is not removed by the larger mass; it simply produces a smaller change in motion. Force remains a vector quantity whether the body is light or heavy.

question: A body’s mass is \(10\,\text{kg}\). The blank is best filled by the SI unit that measures its inertia: \(10\,\_\_\_\_\).
explanation: Mass is measured in kilogram, written as \( \text{kg} \). In mechanics, mass is also used as the measure of inertia. The newton \( \text{N} \) is the unit of force, including weight. The unit \( \text{m s}^{-1} \) belongs to velocity, not inertia. The unit \( \text{kg m s}^{-2} \) is equivalent to \( \text{N} \), so it also represents force. Writing \(10\,\text{kg}\) tells the body’s mass, while its weight would require a value of \(g\).

question: Linear momentum of a body is defined by
explanation: Linear momentum combines the mass of a body with its velocity. Its vector form is \(\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\). Since \(m\) is a scalar and \(\vec{v}\) is a vector, \(\vec{p}\) has the same direction as \(\vec{v}\). The expression \(m\vec{a}\) is related to net force for constant mass, not momentum. The expression \(mg\) gives weight near a gravitational field. Momentum becomes especially useful when studying collisions, impulse, and conservation laws.

question: A \(3\,\text{kg}\) body moves east with velocity \(4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). Its momentum is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Mass \(m=3\,\text{kg}\) and velocity \(\vec{v}=4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) east.
\( \textbf{Required:} \) Momentum \(\vec{p}\).
\( \textbf{Momentum relation:} \)
\[\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\]
Mass is scalar, so it changes the magnitude but not the direction of \(\vec{v}\).
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[\vec{p}=(3\,\text{kg})(4\,\text{m s}^{-1})\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[\vec{p}=12\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
The direction is east because momentum has the same direction as velocity.
The unit \( \text{N} \) would describe force, not momentum.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The momentum is \(12\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) east.

question: A stationary truck has large mass but zero velocity. Its momentum is
opt_c: always greater than that of any moving bicycle
explanation: Momentum is given by \(\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\). If the truck is stationary, its velocity is \(\vec{v}=0\). Therefore \(\vec{p}=m(0)=0\), even though the mass is large. Large mass alone does not produce momentum; motion is also required. Weight is a gravitational force and is not the same as momentum. A moving bicycle can have non-zero momentum because its velocity is non-zero.

question: The SI unit of linear momentum is
explanation: Momentum is defined as \(\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\). The SI unit of mass is \( \text{kg} \), and the SI unit of velocity is \( \text{m s}^{-1} \). Multiplying these units gives \( \text{kg m s}^{-1} \). The unit \( \text{kg m s}^{-2} \) is the newton, which is the unit of force. The unit \( \text{m s}^{-2} \) belongs to acceleration. Momentum and force are related through change of momentum, but their units are not the same.

question: The dimension of momentum is obtained from \(\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\). It is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Momentum relation:} \)
\[\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\]
\( \textbf{Dimension of mass:} \)
\[[m]=[M]\]
\( \textbf{Dimension of velocity:} \)
\[[v]=[LT^{-1}]\]
\( \textbf{Combining dimensions:} \)
\[[p]=[m][v]\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[[p]=[M][LT^{-1}]\]
\( \textbf{Result:} \)
\[[p]=[MLT^{-1}]\]
The dimension \([MLT^{-2}]\) belongs to force.
The difference of one power of \(T\) separates velocity-based momentum from acceleration-based force.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The dimension of momentum is \([MLT^{-1}]\).

question: A \(0.20\,\text{kg}\) ball moving at \(30\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and a \(2.0\,\text{kg}\) cart moving at \(3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) have momenta
explanation:
\( \textbf{Ball data:} \) \(m_b=0.20\,\text{kg}\), \(v_b=30\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Cart data:} \) \(m_c=2.0\,\text{kg}\), \(v_c=3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Momentum relation:} \)
\[p=mv\]
\( \textbf{Ball momentum:} \)
\[p_b=(0.20)(30)=6.0\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Cart momentum:} \)
\[p_c=(2.0)(3)=6.0\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
The fast light ball and the slow heavy cart can have equal momentum because momentum depends on both mass and velocity.
Speed alone or mass alone is not enough for comparison.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) Their momentum magnitudes are equal.

question: A body moving west has momentum directed
opt_b: vertically downward, the same as weight
opt_d: west, the same as its velocity
explanation: Momentum is defined as \(\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\). Mass \(m\) is a positive scalar, so it does not reverse the direction of velocity. Therefore momentum has the same direction as velocity. If the body moves west, its momentum is also westward. Weight may act vertically downward, but that does not decide the direction of momentum. Momentum is a vector quantity, so saying it has no direction is not suitable.

question:
Consider the statements below.
I. Momentum is a vector quantity.
II. The direction of momentum is the same as the direction of velocity.
III. A body with zero velocity can still have non-zero momentum because it has mass.
The suitable set is
explanation: Momentum is a vector because it is the product of mass and velocity, and velocity is a vector. Since mass is a scalar, it does not change the direction of velocity. Therefore the direction of momentum is the same as the direction of velocity. Statement III is not suitable because \(\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\), and if \(\vec{v}=0\), then \(\vec{p}=0\). A body at rest may have mass and inertia, but it has no linear momentum. This separates inertia from momentum: inertia depends on mass, while momentum depends on both mass and velocity.

question: A \(1500\,\text{kg}\) car moving at \(20\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and a \(3000\,\text{kg}\) truck moving at \(10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) travel in the same direction. Their momentum magnitudes are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Car data:} \) \(m_1=1500\,\text{kg}\), \(v_1=20\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Truck data:} \) \(m_2=3000\,\text{kg}\), \(v_2=10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Momentum magnitude:} \)
\[p=mv\]
\( \textbf{Car momentum:} \)
\[p_1=(1500)(20)=30000\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Truck momentum:} \)
\[p_2=(3000)(10)=30000\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
Both are moving in the same direction and have equal momentum magnitudes.
The larger mass of the truck is balanced by the smaller speed in this comparison.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) Both vehicles have equal momentum magnitudes.

question:
Study the table and identify the row that contains an unsuitable statement about momentum.
RowStatement
P\(\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\)
QThe SI unit of momentum is \( \text{kg m s}^{-1} \)
RMomentum has the same direction as velocity
SMomentum of a stationary body equals its weight
explanation: Row P is suitable because momentum is defined as \(\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\). Row Q is also suitable because multiplying \( \text{kg} \) by \( \text{m s}^{-1} \) gives \( \text{kg m s}^{-1} \). Row R is suitable because mass is scalar, so momentum follows the direction of velocity. Row S is not suitable because a stationary body has \(\vec{v}=0\), so its momentum is zero. Weight is a force given by \(W=mg\), and it has unit \( \text{N} \). A body can have weight while having zero momentum if it is at rest.

question: Change in linear momentum is represented by
explanation: Change in any vector quantity is final value minus initial value. For linear momentum, the initial momentum is \(\vec{p}_1\) and the final momentum is \(\vec{p}_2\). Therefore the change in momentum is \(\Delta\vec{p}=\vec{p}_2-\vec{p}_1\). Since momentum is a vector, this subtraction must include direction, not only magnitude. Simply adding \(\vec{p}_1\) and \(\vec{p}_2\) would give a different vector quantity. Direction becomes especially important when a body reverses direction or rebounds.

question: A \(2\,\text{kg}\) body moving east at \(3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) speeds up to \(7\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) east. The change in its momentum is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Mass \(m=2\,\text{kg}\), initial velocity \(\vec{v}_1=3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) east, and final velocity \(\vec{v}_2=7\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) east.
\( \textbf{Required:} \) Change in momentum \(\Delta\vec{p}\).
Since both velocities are eastward, take east as positive.
\( \textbf{Initial momentum:} \)
\[\vec{p}_1=m\vec{v}_1=(2)(3)=6\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Final momentum:} \)
\[\vec{p}_2=m\vec{v}_2=(2)(7)=14\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Change in momentum:} \)
\[\Delta\vec{p}=\vec{p}_2-\vec{p}_1\]
\[\Delta\vec{p}=14-6=8\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
The positive sign shows that the change is eastward.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The change in momentum is \(8\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) east.

question: A ball of mass \(0.5\,\text{kg}\) moving north at \(6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) is brought to rest. Its change in momentum is
opt_d: zero because the final velocity is zero
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m=0.5\,\text{kg}\), \(\vec{v}_1=6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) north, and \(\vec{v}_2=0\).
Take north as positive.
\( \textbf{Initial momentum:} \)
\[\vec{p}_1=m\vec{v}_1=(0.5)(6)=3\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Final momentum:} \)
\[\vec{p}_2=m\vec{v}_2=0\]
\( \textbf{Change in momentum:} \)
\[\Delta\vec{p}=\vec{p}_2-\vec{p}_1\]
\[\Delta\vec{p}=0-3=-3\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
The negative sign means the change in momentum is toward south.
A body brought to rest has zero final momentum, but its change in momentum is not zero.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The change in momentum is \(3\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) south.

question: A body can have a change in momentum even when its speed remains constant if
opt_b: it is observed for a longer time only
explanation: Momentum is a vector quantity given by \(\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\). Since velocity is a vector, momentum depends on both speed and direction. If a body changes direction while keeping the same speed, its velocity changes. Therefore its momentum also changes. Uniform circular motion is a common case where speed can remain constant while momentum changes continuously. The unit \( \text{kg} \) for mass does not by itself cause any change in momentum.

question: A \(1\,\text{kg}\) ball moving east at \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) rebounds and moves west at \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). Taking east as positive, its change in momentum is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) Mass \(m=1\,\text{kg}\).
East is taken as positive, so the initial velocity is \(+5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
After rebounding, the ball moves west, so the final velocity is \(-5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Initial momentum:} \)
\[\vec{p}_1=m\vec{v}_1=(1)(+5)=+5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Final momentum:} \)
\[\vec{p}_2=m\vec{v}_2=(1)(-5)=-5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Change in momentum:} \)
\[\Delta\vec{p}=\vec{p}_2-\vec{p}_1\]
\[\Delta\vec{p}=-5-(+5)=-10\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
The magnitude of the change is \(10\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\), directed west.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The change in momentum is \(-10\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).

question:
Study the table and identify the row that gives a suitable momentum-change statement.
RowMotion changeMomentum change
PSpeed increases in the same directionMomentum magnitude increases
QSpeed becomes zeroMomentum must remain unchanged
RDirection reverses at the same speedMomentum change is zero
SDirection changes at constant speedMomentum cannot change
explanation: Momentum magnitude is \(p=mv\), so if mass is constant and speed increases in the same direction, momentum magnitude increases. Row Q is not suitable because a body brought to rest has final momentum zero, so its momentum generally changes. Row R is not suitable because reversing direction produces a large vector change in momentum even if speed is unchanged. Row S is also not suitable because changing direction changes velocity and therefore changes momentum. Momentum must be treated as a vector, so direction cannot be ignored. Row P is the only row that keeps both magnitude and direction reasoning consistent.

question: A \(0.10\,\text{kg}\) rubber ball hits a wall with velocity \(20\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) east and rebounds with velocity \(15\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) west. Taking east as positive, the change in momentum is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given:} \) \(m=0.10\,\text{kg}\), \(\vec{v}_1=+20\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), and \(\vec{v}_2=-15\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
East is positive, so west is negative.
\( \textbf{Initial momentum:} \)
\[\vec{p}_1=m\vec{v}_1=(0.10)(+20)\]
\[\vec{p}_1=+2.0\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Final momentum:} \)
\[\vec{p}_2=m\vec{v}_2=(0.10)(-15)\]
\[\vec{p}_2=-1.5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
\( \textbf{Change in momentum:} \)
\[\Delta\vec{p}=\vec{p}_2-\vec{p}_1\]
\[\Delta\vec{p}=-1.5-(+2.0)\]
\[\Delta\vec{p}=-3.5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\]
The negative sign shows that the change is toward west.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The change in momentum is \(-3.5\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).

question:
Read the case below and answer the question.
A small cart moves along a straight track. In Case P, its speed changes from \(2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) east to \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) east. In Case Q, its speed remains \(2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), but its direction changes from east to north.
What is the best conclusion?
opt_a: Momentum changes only in Case P
opt_b: Momentum changes only in Case Q
explanation: Momentum is \(\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\), so it depends on the velocity vector. In Case P, the direction remains east but the speed changes from \(2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) to \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), so the momentum magnitude changes. In Case Q, the speed is unchanged but the direction changes from east to north. Since velocity changes when direction changes, momentum also changes. The two cases show two different ways of changing momentum. A comparison based only on speed would miss the vector nature of momentum.

question: In a momentum calculation, a body changes velocity from \(+4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) to \(-4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). For constant mass \(m\), the change in momentum is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial velocity:} \) \(v_1=+4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Final velocity:} \) \(v_2=-4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Momentum change relation:} \)
\[\Delta p=p_2-p_1\]
For constant mass:
\[\Delta p=m(v_2-v_1)\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[\Delta p=m[(-4)-(+4)]\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[\Delta p=m(-8)\]
\[\Delta p=-8m\]
The answer is not zero because the velocity direction has reversed.
The sign shows that the change is in the negative direction.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The change in momentum is \(-8m\).

question:
A graph description is given below.
For a moving body of constant mass, the momentum-time graph is a horizontal straight line.
This graph shows that
opt_d: the velocity must be changing direction continuously
explanation: A horizontal straight line on a momentum-time graph means the momentum value does not change with time. Since momentum is constant, \(\Delta\vec{p}=0\) over any chosen time interval on that graph. For a body of constant mass, this also means velocity is constant in both magnitude and direction. The graph does not show zero mass; it only shows no change in momentum. It also does not show continuous direction change, because direction change would change the momentum vector. The physical reading of the horizontal graph is unchanged momentum.

question: For a body of constant mass \(m\), the relation connecting change in momentum and change in velocity is
explanation: Momentum is defined as \(\vec{p}=m\vec{v}\). If mass remains constant, the change in momentum comes only from the change in velocity. Therefore \(\Delta\vec{p}=m\Delta\vec{v}\). This relation is vector-based, so \(\Delta\vec{v}\) must include direction changes as well as speed changes. The expression \(\frac{\Delta\vec{v}}{m}\) has unsuitable physical meaning for momentum change. The term \(mg\Delta t\) may appear in a gravitational impulse context later, but it is not the general definition of change in momentum.

question: A moving ball turns through a right angle without changing speed. Its initial momentum is eastward with magnitude \(p\), and its final momentum is northward with magnitude \(p\). The magnitude of change in momentum is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial momentum:} \) Magnitude \(p\) toward east.
\( \textbf{Final momentum:} \) Magnitude \(p\) toward north.
The change in momentum is
\[\Delta\vec{p}=\vec{p}_2-\vec{p}_1\]
East and north are perpendicular directions.
The vector \(\Delta\vec{p}\) is found from the difference between two perpendicular vectors of equal magnitude.
\( \textbf{Magnitude relation:} \)
\[|\Delta\vec{p}|=\sqrt{p^2+p^2}\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[|\Delta\vec{p}|=\sqrt{2p^2}\]
\[|\Delta\vec{p}|=\sqrt{2}p\]
The change is not zero because the direction of momentum has changed.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The magnitude of change in momentum is \(\sqrt{2}p\).

question: A body is said to obey Newton’s first law when, in the absence of a non-zero net external force, it
explanation: Newton’s first law states that a body remains in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by a non-zero net external force. The phrase “net external force” is important because individual forces may act and still balance one another. If the body is at rest, it remains at rest when the net force is zero. If it is already moving with constant velocity in a straight line, it continues that motion. The law does not say that motion must fade away by itself. It links change in motion with a non-zero resultant external force.

question: A box rests on a floor. Its weight acts downward and the normal reaction from the floor acts upward with equal magnitude. Newton’s first law predicts that the box
opt_a: remains at rest if no other unbalanced force acts
opt_b: must move upward because the normal reaction acts upward
opt_c: must move downward because weight is a force
opt_d: must move horizontally because two forces act on it
explanation: The weight of the box and the normal reaction both act on the box. If they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, their vector sum is zero. With zero net force and initial rest, Newton’s first law says the box remains at rest. The presence of two forces does not automatically produce motion; the resultant force matters. The upward normal force alone should not be considered without the downward weight. This is an example of rest under balanced forces.

question: A spacecraft is far from planets and moves with constant velocity after its engines are switched off. Ignoring external forces, the motion is best explained by
opt_b: force being stored inside the spacecraft
explanation: Newton’s first law applies when the net external force on a body is zero or negligible. A spacecraft already moving in deep space can continue with constant velocity without needing a continuous forward thrust. Switching off the engines removes the thrust, but it does not remove the existing velocity. Since no significant external force is assumed, there is no acceleration. This does not mean force is stored inside the spacecraft. The example separates the maintenance of uniform motion from the need for force to change motion.

question:
Consider the statements below.
I. Newton’s first law is also called the law of inertia.
II. A body moving with uniform velocity has zero acceleration.
III. Zero net force always means the body has zero velocity.
The suitable set is
explanation: Newton’s first law is called the law of inertia because it describes the tendency of a body to preserve its state of rest or uniform straight-line motion. Statement II is also suitable because uniform velocity means no change in the velocity vector, so acceleration is zero. Statement III is not suitable because zero net force means zero acceleration, not necessarily zero velocity. A body can move with constant non-zero velocity when the net force is zero. The law includes both rest and uniform straight-line motion as possible unchanged states. The distinction between velocity and acceleration is central to applying the first law.

question:
Assertion: A body moving with constant velocity in a straight line may have zero net force acting on it.
Reason: A non-zero net force is required to change velocity, not to maintain uniform velocity.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: A body moving with constant velocity has zero acceleration. Newton’s first law says that uniform straight-line motion can continue when no non-zero net external force acts. Therefore the Assertion is true. The Reason correctly explains the role of net force: it is needed to change velocity, not to maintain a velocity that is already constant. This is why uniform motion and rest are treated together as states that persist when the net force is zero. The wording must refer to net force, because balanced forces can act while the resultant remains zero.

question: A puck moving on a smooth horizontal surface enters a region where no horizontal force acts. Its path in that region will be
opt_b: a straight line with constant velocity
opt_c: a zigzag path because force is absent
opt_d: a straight line with speed decreasing to zero immediately
explanation: If no horizontal force acts, the horizontal acceleration is zero. With zero acceleration, the puck’s horizontal velocity remains unchanged. Therefore it continues along a straight line with constant velocity. A circular path would require a force toward the centre to change the direction of velocity. A zigzag path also requires changes in direction, so it cannot occur without forces causing those changes. The puck does not stop immediately because zero net force does not mean zero velocity.

question: In Newton’s first law, the phrase “unless acted upon by a net external force” is used because
opt_a: any single force always disappears during motion
opt_b: velocity and force are the same physical quantity
opt_c: force has no effect on acceleration
opt_d: net external force changes system motion
explanation: Newton’s first law is concerned with whether the resultant external force can change the state of motion. If forces on a body balance, their net effect is zero and the body’s velocity does not change. For a system, internal forces occur between parts of the system and may not change the motion of the system as a whole. This is why the word “net” and the word “external” are both important. A single force does not disappear just because motion exists. The law says that acceleration is connected with a non-zero net external force.

question: A velocity-time graph for a body is a straight horizontal line below the time axis. The best first-law interpretation is that the body
opt_a: is at rest because the graph is horizontal
opt_b: has constant negative velocity and zero acceleration
opt_c: has a continuously increasing force in the negative direction
opt_d: has zero velocity because acceleration is zero
explanation: A horizontal line on a velocity-time graph means constant velocity. Since the line is below the time axis, the velocity is in the chosen negative direction. The slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration, and a horizontal line has zero slope. Therefore the acceleration is zero. Newton’s first-law interpretation is that the net force along that line is zero if the mass is constant and no other changing condition is involved. Zero acceleration does not require the velocity itself to be zero, so the position of the line relative to the time axis matters.

question: A frame of reference in which Newton’s first law holds without adding any extra force is called
explanation: An inertial frame is a frame in which a body with zero net external force remains at rest or continues in uniform straight-line motion. In such a frame, Newton’s first law is valid in its usual form. The frame itself is not accelerating in a way that creates apparent changes in motion. For many problems, the ground is treated as approximately inertial when Earth’s rotation and other small effects are ignored. A frame name is not decided by temperature, magnetism, or deformation. The key test is whether the first-law behaviour is observed without introducing an extra apparent force.

question: A bus suddenly accelerates forward, and a standing passenger seems to fall backward relative to the bus. The bus frame during this acceleration is best treated as
opt_a: an inertial frame because the passenger appears to move
opt_b: a non-inertial frame because the bus accelerates
opt_c: an inertial frame because Earth attracts the passenger
opt_d: a frame with no possible laws of motion
explanation: The bus frame is accelerating forward, so it is not an inertial frame during that interval. A passenger who was initially at rest tends to remain in the earlier state of motion because of inertia. Relative to the accelerating bus, the passenger appears to move backward. This apparent backward tendency is not caused by a real backward contact force on the whole body. In a ground frame, the explanation can be given using inertia and contact forces from the bus floor. The same event can look different in different frames, so the nature of the chosen frame matters.
